title: The Thunderbird and the Whale
summary: The Thunderbird, lord of the sky, wages eternal war against the Great Whale, lord of the sea — and their battle is the storm.
full_text:
In the time before time, the sky and the sea were one. There was no horizon, no line between water and air. Everything was a single, swirling darkness.

Then the Thunderbird was born. It burst from the darkness like lightning — a bird so large that its wingspan covered the sky. Its feathers were black iron, and its eyes were the color of lightning. When it beat its wings, thunder rolled across the world. When it opened its beak, fire poured forth.

The Thunderbird looked down and saw the water. It was dark, vast, and deep. Something moved in it — something enormous. The Great Whale, lord of the sea, rose from the depths. Its body was the size of an island. Its blowhole was a volcano. Its tail was a tsunami.

The Thunderbird and the Great Whale looked at each other. They were the only two beings in the world, and they were both immense, and they were both alone.

The Thunderbird swooped. The Great Whale leaped. They met in the space between sky and sea — the first horizon. The Thunderbird's talons closed around the Whale's back. The Whale's tail struck the Thunderbird's chest. They wrestled, and the world shook.

The battle lasted for days. The Thunderbird struck with lightning. The Whale struck with waves. Where the lightning hit the water, steam rose in columns. Where the waves hit the sky, clouds formed. The first rain fell from their struggle — hot at first, then cold.

The Thunderbird was winning. Its talons dug into the Whale's flesh, and the Whale screamed — a sound like a foghorn, like a glacier calving, like the ocean itself in pain. The blood of the Whale was black, and where it fell, the water turned dark.

The Whale made one final effort. It dove. It pulled the Thunderbird down, down, down into the black water. The Thunderbird fought. Its wings beat the surface into foam. Its lightning lit the underwater darkness. But the sea was deep, and the Whale was home.

The Thunderbird could not breathe underwater. Its lightning sputtered. Its wings grew heavy. It was drowning.

Then the Thunderbird did something desperate. It called to the sky. It screamed — a sound like a thousand thunderbolts — and the sky answered. The clouds gathered. The wind rose. The rain poured down in sheets. And with the rain came the rivers — every river in the world, flowing downhill, carrying the Thunderbird upward, out of the water, back to the sky.

The Great Whale released its grip. The Thunderbird flew free, dripping, wounded, but alive. It flew to the highest peak and perched there, exhausted. The Whale swam to the deepest trench and lay there, bleeding.

They have not fought since. But they have not forgotten.

Every summer, when the Thunderbird flies south, the sky darkens and the lightning strikes. The Whale rises in the deep, and the waves grow tall. The sailors call it a storm. The Tlingit know better.

It is the Thunderbird and the Whale, fighting their eternal war. The lightning is the Thunderbird's talons. The waves are the Whale's tail. And the rain is the blood of their struggle — hot at first, then cold.

One day, they will fight again. The Thunderbird will swoop. The Whale will leap. And the world will shake as it did in the beginning.

Until then, the storms keep the balance between sky and sea.
moral: The balance of the world is maintained by opposing forces. Without the storm, there is no rain. Without the battle, there is no horizon.
source: Based on Tlingit and Pacific Northwest coast oral traditions.
